The Best Meal of My Life
Aug 2024 • Friends
This experience was nothing short of extraordinary. I've indulged in countless omakase meals around the world, including some of the finest in Japan and New York, but this one stands in a league of its own. I can’t recommend this place highly enough. The meal itself was a masterpiece, and the level of service and attention to detail was simply unparalleled. Chef Chu didn’t just serve us; he guided us through each course with a deep sense of care and passion, taking the time to know us personally and offering invaluable recommendations for our stay.

We opted for the special omakase, and the value for money was beyond impressive. As Americans abroad, navigating a country where English isn't widely spoken, it was a rare and comforting pleasure to converse with Chu, who shared his fascinating experiences from both the US and Vietnam, having worked at some of LA’s most prestigious Japanese restaurants.

In a lifetime of traveling to over 30 countries with the singular goal of tasting the world’s best food, this meal is undoubtedly one of the most unforgettable. I feel incredibly fortunate to have discovered this gem. In a city brimming with omakase options, **this** is the place to go. Whenever anyone asks for recommendations in Vietnam, this is the first place I tell them they absolutely must visit. It’s outstanding, and you will carry the memory of this meal with you forever.

Kasen Omakase
It's obvious this foreign national has visited a lot of the Japanese places in Saigon, and amassed a sophisticated vocabulary.

As a refresher, here is a quick tip on when you know you're at a Vietnamese restaurant that serves sushi:

- Greeted by a girl wearing kimono that looks like an ao dai and everyone screams in Japanese they don't understand

- Plastic food on display showing ramen, fried shrimp, Thai hot pot, rubber fish and pho noodles

- Neoprene cherry blossoms bloom over each table

- Non-alcohol drinks are adorned with curvy straws, blue, red, green colors and lots of local fruit.

- Hot Hanoi sake served in the middle of a heat wave

- 10 pages of salmon in a picture menu as thick as the Bible

- Pink ginger

- Neon Green Clay wasabi

- Sashimi eaten in half soy sauce and 1 kg of wasabi

- Fried batter served as tempura

- Sushi made from rolled avocado, lettuce, pineapple, cucumber, basil, egg, thyme, cilantro and seaweed topped with fish sauce and mayonnaise

- Pink ginger topped on every piece of sushi

- Big boats full of white smoke and cut river fish of unknown origin (you really think that fish is from Hokkaido?)

- Chinese hot pot to end the meal

- don't forget buy 4 and 1 free beer

- did I mention the pink ginger?

The food is cheap because its cheap. It's your choice to eat street sushi at Hokkaido sach but never dare tell our guests otherwise. Me entiendes, foolish one!

Soft product: excellent. Hard product: could be better.
Dec 2020
Kasen is one of a handful of Omakase style restaurants in Saigon and is definitely worth a visit. The fish I was served tasted fresh and relatively speaking — the prices were reasonable. My guest and I had the 11-course seasonal menu which was just under US$60 per person. Mind you, most omakase restaurants the world over are often twice that amount and then some. 

Unlike some of the reviewers here, I’ve only been to two other omakase restaurants (Sushi Rei in Saigon and Sushi Masato in Bangkok). And I’ve never been to Japan (for what it’s worth). 

As I mentioned above, the food was delicious and the service was warm and understated. I thought the pacing of the dishes was good too. 

My complaint is mostly about the physical space of the restaurant. Part of the pleasure of being served at a sushi bar is watching the chefs create your food. Unfortunately, the bar at Kasen is so high, that you can hardly see over it without standing up and moving your body forward. I’d suggest lowering the bar so people can actually see the chefs in action. 

My second complaint is the lighting. Boy is it bright in there. Having lived in Vietnam for over 5 years I realize that people here don’t focus much on ‘mood lighting’ — everything has to be lit as though we’re in a shopping mall. Dim the lights, focus them on the chefs preparing the food and that’s all. Good lighting is important. 

Lastly — music. It was distracting hearing pop, rock, and other random music play in the background (even though I love Fleetwood Mac). May I suggest some modern ambient music? It's picayune, I know, but both my friend and I were thinking the same thing. It was just incongruous with the setting and the food. 

My three gripes might seem silly, but when you’re spending money at a restaurant like this, it’s not just about the food — it’s the environment and experience. 

I’ve read some of the caustic (often amusing) responses from the owner (or) manager on here so I can only imagine what he’ll say…
